question: A technical writer's system prompt says "NEVER use ellipses", but Claude occasionally still uses them in unusual contexts. The real reason for the rule is that Claude's responses are read aloud by a text-to-speech engine, and the writer has not told Claude that. The writer wants Claude to generalize the rule reliably. What should they add to the instruction?
options: A) Explain that the text-to-speech engine reading the responses aloud cannot pronounce ellipses
B) Add several more exclamation marks to the instruction to emphasize how important the rule is
C) Replace the instruction with a much longer list of every punctuation mark Claude should avoid
D) Ask Claude to run a careful spell-check pass after the response to catch any stray ellipses
correct_answers: A) Explain that the text-to-speech engine reading the responses aloud cannot pronounce ellipses
explanations: Correct. Anthropic's prompting guidance says that providing the context or motivation behind an instruction helps Claude understand the goal, and its own example pairs a bare ban on ellipses with the reason that a text-to-speech engine cannot pronounce them. Knowing the reason lets Claude generalize the rule to cases the writer did not anticipate.
Adding emphasis through extra punctuation or capitalization does not tell Claude why the rule exists, so it does not help Claude generalize to edge cases the writer never listed.
Listing more banned punctuation marks addresses symptoms rather than the underlying reason, and still would not cover every unanticipated case.
A separate post-generation check adds an extra step but does not address why Claude keeps producing ellipses in the first place, because Claude still does not know the purpose of the rule.
